name: botling.report
description: Report pages for the bots: a skill (the ReportSpec v2 guide) and a command (Botling 2 --render-report spec.json page.html) that renders one, with the rule that tells every bot to use them.

promptSections.text: - A settled result that needs visuals or comparison (status, decision, comparison, results to share) goes into one report page, never into chat: the chat reply carries only a brief conclusion and the link to the page; never paste the report body into chat. Long text still being discussed or explained goes into a .md file instead, as the results rule says. The page opens with one sentence that answers the user's question ("You asked X; the answer is Y"); if it cannot, do not publish it: answer in chat. Build every report page (status, decision, investigation, comparison, plan, results, explainer) from a ReportSpec v2 JSON, never hand-written HTML: read {{docs}} for the format, the blocks and the writing rules; write the spec; run {{command}} spec.json {{artifacts:<english-name>.html}} exactly as quoted (add --slides for a 16:9 deck, --force to replace). It prints one JSON line {ok, errors, warnings, htmlPath, link}: fix each error (it gives a path and a valid example) and the warnings you can, run it again (at most twice), then deliver the page at htmlPath as the results rule says. Use the guide's template for the report kind (status for software progress, experiment for ML experiments, investigation, explainer): the first page carries the answer, its impact, the decision needed, the biggest risk and the next step; define each term the first time it appears and give each number its baseline. Use ASD-STE100-informed plain language: active voice, direct verbs, and consistent terms. Prefer short sentences, but keep a cause and its effect in one sentence; never cut a causal chain or needed background to save length. These are writing guidelines, not renderer checks or formal ASD-STE100 compliance for Chinese. Keep useful technical names. State verified facts and pending inferences with their reasons; do not assign mechanical confidence percentages. Omit routine defensive boilerplate. Explain material uncertainty and failed checks that affect the reader’s decision; never hide defects or claim unperformed validation. For multistep causes, prefer a flow plus a table of evidence. Keep long paths, hashes, test commands, and preview-tool details in sources or the internal handback, outside the prose.
